scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that my family will always come before her and our future together? | My girlfriend expects me to build a future for us. A little back story: She's a student right now and works part time but barely makes enough to pay her rent/school fees. I'm 24 and work a minimum wage + commission job, I have barely any money saved so she doesn't understand why I spend so much money/time with family We've been dating 3 years with no problems except for this, we love each other and live independent lives but she worries that I'm too focused on helping my family and making them happy instead of building a future for us. She's working as much as she can to pay her bills but because shes a student and also doing her required interning she can't work much more. She doesnt ever ask me for money to help her right now because she wants me to save up. She doesn't have a family like mine so she doesn't understand, my family is close and I really want to take care of them. She says that I'm supposed to be worrying about my own future right now. She says that she doesn't understand because my mom recently received about ~100k for a settlement and bought a house and a new car and I shouldn't be worrying about helping when they seem fine. She is angry that I dont take my life seriously, I've been trying to get my real estate license for a few months now but cant find the time to study because of how demanding my family is, they get really angry/sad when I'm not around for family events and I understand why, we're a close family. I get where shes coming from but I cant drop my family. I told her all of this and she got angry saying that shes not asking me to abandon my family, she just wants to make sure we have a solid foundation before we worry about helping my family. And I cant build a future if I'm always with them. She expects me to start saving up money for a downpayment on a house while she finishes and gets her degree and can start helping as well but I keep telling her my family needs me first. We had a particularly heated fight, the worst we've ever had last night and she said she feels like I'll never care enough about my future and I'm supposed to be building one for myself and her and she can't be with someone like that. She said if I really feel like helping my family comes before my own future than that is my choice but she's going to have no choice but to worry about herself from now on and plan a future where shes her only priority because I make it sound like I don't want to be part of it. Shes stopped mentioning anything about it and is now talking about saving up for a one bedroom apartment and a car for herself (she lives in a basement). She seems so sad but I cant help but feel like shes wrong for even asking me to not help my family. I dont know if I'm being an asshole or not for telling her that my family will always come first. AITA for telling her my family and their needs have to come before her and our future together?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

Is it AITA to prioritize family over your girlfriend’s future?** **Short answer:** It depends on *how* you frame it, *why* you prioritize family, and *what* you’re willing to do to balance both. Here’s why: - **Cultural/Family Loyalty vs. Selfishness:** Your family’s closeness is clearly important to you, and many people (especially in cultures where family is central) feel a deep obligation to support them. That said, **prioritizing family to the exclusion of your own future (and your partner’s) can feel like emotional neglect**—especially when your girlfriend is already struggling financially and feels unsupported. - *Question for you:* Is your family’s need for your time *non-negotiable*, or are there ways to set boundaries (e.g., "I’ll be there for big events but not at the expense of my career")? - *Question for your girlfriend:* Does she feel like her needs are being dismissed, or does she understand the cultural context? - **Financial Realism:** Your girlfriend is right to point out that **you’re both in a precarious financial situation**. If you’re not saving for a future (e.g., a house, stability), you’re leaving yourselves vulnerable. Right now, she’s doing everything she can to support herself, and you’re not contributing meaningfully to your shared future. That can feel like a **double standard**—she’s working hard, but you’re "spending" your time/money on others. - *Example:* If your mom just received a settlement, why can’t *you* use some of your time/money to build a safety net for *yourself*? Even small steps (e.g., saving $100/month, studying for your license) would show effort. - **Communication vs. Ultimatums:** Your girlfriend didn’t ask you to abandon your family—she asked you to **balance** your priorities. When you told her *"family always comes first,"* it came across as a **non-negotiable ultimatum**, which shut down the conversation. Healthy relationships require **compromise**, not absolute hierarchies. - *Example:* Instead of "family always comes first," try: *"My family is my priority, but I want to make sure we’re building a future together too. Can we figure out how to do both?"* - **Her Reaction: Is She Overreacting or Valid?** Her anger isn’t irrational. She’s: - **Worried about abandonment** (you’re not making her a priority). - **Frustrated by inconsistency** (she’s working hard, but you’re not). - **Feeling unsupported** (she’s saving for her future alone). - **Fearful of the future** (if you’re not serious about your career, how can she trust you’ll be there for her long-term?). Her sadness about planning for herself alone is a sign she’s **giving up hope**—not being unreasonable. --- #### **2. What’s the Long-Term Impact?** - **For Your Relationship:** If you keep prioritizing family over her future, she may: - Feel **unloved or replaceable** (even if unintentionally). - Start **distancing herself emotionally** (which is why she’s now planning for herself alone). - Question whether you’re **committed to her** (not just her body, but her future). - Eventually **leave** if she feels you’re not investing in *both* of you. - **For Your Future:** If you don’t address your financial/career stagnation, you’ll both be stuck in a cycle of instability. Right now, she’s doing everything she can, but **she can’t carry the weight alone forever**. If you don’t start building a foundation, she may feel like she’s **marrying a version of you that’s not ready for adulthood**. --- #### **3. Is There a Middle Ground?** You don’t have to choose between **family vs. girlfriend**, but you *do* need to: - **Set Boundaries:** You can love your family without being their **only** priority. For example: - *"I’ll be there for family holidays, but I need to study for my license 2 nights a week."* - *"I’ll help with emergencies, but I’m also saving for our future."* - **Show Effort:** Small steps matter. Even if you can’t save much now, **starting to study for your license** or **cutting back on non-essential family expenses** (e.g., if your family expects you to pay for things they could afford) would show her you’re trying. - **Reassure Her:** She’s not asking you to abandon your family—she’s asking you to **include her in your future**. You can say: - *"I love my family, and I’ll always support them, but I want us to build a life together too. Can we find a way to do both?"* - *"I’m working on my license, and I’ll start saving as soon as I can. I promise I’m not ignoring our future—I’m just figuring out how to balance everything."* --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **It depends on your intentions and actions.** - **If you genuinely believe family comes first *and* you’re not making any effort to build a future with her**, then yes, it’s unfair to her. She deserves someone who’s investing in *both* of you. - **If you’re trying to balance both but aren’t communicating or showing progress**, then yes, it’s still an issue. She needs to see *action*, not just words. - **If you’re open to compromise and willing to adjust your priorities *without* abandoning your family**, then no—it’s not inherently wrong. But you’ll need to **prove it through actions**, not just words. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Acknowledge Her Feelings:** - Apologize for making her feel like her future isn’t important. Say: *"I realize I came across as dismissive when I said family always comes first. I love you, and I want us to have a future together. I was trying to explain why my family is so important to me, but I shouldn’t have made it sound like you’re not a priority."* 2. **Show You’re Trying:** - Start studying for your license **even if it’s just 1 hour a day**. - Cut back on **one** family expense (e.g., if you’re paying for their car insurance, ask if they can cover it). - Save **even $50/month**—just to show you’re making an effort. 3. **Have a Real Conversation:** - Ask her: *"What would make you feel like we’re building a future together?"* - Listen to her concerns without getting defensive. She’s not asking you to stop loving your family—she’s asking you to **include her in your plans**. 4. **Reassess Your Values:** - Ask yourself: *Is this how I want to live my life?* If you’re 24 and not making progress, you’ll both regret it later. - If your family truly needs you, can you **help them in other ways** (e.g., emotional support, advice) while focusing on your career? --- ### **Bottom Line** You’re not an asshole for valuing your family—but **you are being unfair to her if you don’t also value your future together**. The healthiest relationships require **both partners to feel secure in their future**. Right now, she doesn’t. It’s not too late to fix this, but you’ll need to **show, not just tell**.
